name: Ushojo
confidence_why: The only description of Ushojo, Decker 1992, says outright that no phonological analysis was done and that tone was not analysed, its word list marks stress on varying syllables without stating a rule, and Baart c. 2003 only suspects the language is tonal, so nothing about Ushojo word stress can be stated with confidence.

Hallberg, Languages of Kohistan (Sociolinguistic Survey of Northern Pakistan 1), 65-80 and Appendix C (Ushojo survey data) 193-206. Islamabad: National Institute of Pakistan Studies & Summer Institute of Linguistics. (SIL archive 38565; read from an Internet Archive snapshot of 2024-05-23.)
catalog_locator: Section 7.2 Tone, p. 75; Section 7.1 preamble, p. 72; Appendix A.1 note p. 146 and phonetic-chart key p. 147; Appendix C.1 Ushojo word list, Karial, Swat, pp. 193-195.
catalog_quote: 7.2 Tone. An analysis of tone in Ushojo was not attempted. Use of Computerized Extraction of Components of Intonation in Language (CECIL) (Hunt 1990) indicates there is some sort of tone factor at work in Ushojo. Based on the work of Schmidt, who has identified three tonemes in Palas Shina (Schmidt 1981:170), it would seem possible that tone is distinctive. [p. 75] ... The following charts are a listing of the phonetic sounds found in the Ushojo data. A complete phonological analysis has not been done. ... These remarks should be interpreted as preliminary hypotheses, requiring more extensive field work before phonological conclusions can be confidently proposed. [p. 72] ... It should be noted that the word list data and transcribed texts as included in the subsequent appendices are field transcriptions and have not undergone thorough phonological and grammatical analysis. [p. 146] ... [zV'bàn] stress [p. 147, transcription key]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: opened (285 pp., text; SIL SSNP01 metadata) and re-extracted pp. 94-97 = printed pp. 72-75. Section 7.2 Tone, p. 75 (p. 97) reads exactly: "An analysis of tone in Ushojo was not attempted. Use of Computerized Extraction of Components of Intonation in Language (CECIL) (Hunt 1990) indicates there is some sort of tone factor at work in Ushojo. Based on the work of Schmidt, who has identified three tonemes in Palas Shina (Schmidt 1981:170), it would seem possible that tone is distinctive." Section 7.1, p. 72 (p. 94) reads exactly: "The following charts are a listing of the phonetic sounds found in the Ushojo data. A complete phonological analysis has not been done." Both halves of…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word-stress placement is stated anywhere. The only prosodic statement is that Ushojo may be a tone language (as its relative Palas Shina is, with three tonemes), on the strength of unanalysed CECIL pitch traces; the author explicitly declines a phonological analysis. The survey word list transcribes a stress mark (') on many words in varying positions (initial 'wàjuth, 'mànuZ7o; final cV'Tu, sV'TVk, VKgu'Ti, às'màn), which suggests stress/pitch prominence is not fixed to one syllable in the transcriber's hearing, but that is an inference from raw data, not a statement in the source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the whole section is flagged as preliminary hypotheses requiring further fieldwork.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms from a 210-item survey word list (Karial, Swat) plus one narrative text; no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Decker 1992 describes the Ushojo of Karial and Bishigram villages, Chail valley, Swat (word list from Karial); the Hindu Kush Areal Typology data are from a speaker from Chail, Swat. Both are the same variety as Glottolog usho1238; no dialect split is reported. Speakers are a Shina-group community settled among Torwali speakers.

Nothing on word-stress placement. The 210-item word list (Appendix C.1, pp. 193-198) marks stress with a preceding apostrophe (key p. 147) in varying positions ('wàjuth body, cV'Tu mortar, sV'TVk hammer, VKgu'Ti ring, às'màn sky, 'mànuZ7o man); the text in C.3 is unmarked. sources.citation: Liljegren, Henrik, Robert Forkel, Nina Knobloch & Noa Lange. 2026. Hindu Kush Areal Typology, CLDF dataset v1.1.0 (Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.21406260; web apphttps://hindukush.clld.org/languages/ush;GitHub cldf-datasets/liljegrenhindukush). Ushojo data elicited Islamabad, Oct 2015, consultant AH.
sources.note: The 80 structural features include a phonology block PH01-PH08 (retroflexion, affricates, syllable structure, aspiration, uvulars, nasal vowels, inventory size) but no tone, stress or accent feature; the 213 Ushojo wordlist forms are in IPA without any stress or tone marks. Silent on stress.
No phonology, stress or tone information; its references pointed to the SIL archive entry 38565 for Decker 1992 and the FLI Ushojo Alifbe PDF.

sources.citation: Liljegren, Henrik. 2017. Profiling Indo-Aryan in the Hindukush-Karakoram: A preliminary study of micro-typological patterns. Journal of South Asian Languages and Linguistics 4(1): 107-156.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Ushojo is in the sample with Liljegren's own 2015 elicitation and the paper scores a Tone feature (none / 2-way Shina-type / 3-way / 4+-way), but prints only aggregate counts; the per-language Ushojo value would be the only first-hand post-1992 prosodic judgement and is not in the paper text or in the HKAT v1.1.0 CLDF feature set (PH01-PH08). Worth asking the author for the underlying tone coding if a tone note for Ushojo is ever staged.

sources.citation: Baart, Joan L. G. c. 2002/2003. Tonal features in languages of northern Pakistan. Conference paper (SIL/NIPS), 13 pp; PDF formerly athttp://www.geocities.ws/kcs_kalam/tonefeat.pdf
sources.note: Survey of tone in 30 languages of northern Pakistan. Table 1 (p. 3) lists 'Ushojo Yes? 2,000' (tone suspected, not established). Pp. 6-7: 'Ushojo may be an interesting case for investigating the effect of language contact on tone. This language has not yet been studied very well and we do not know much about it.' Nothing on stress placement; second-hand.
